Family Health

Penile fracture: emergency signs, treatment and recovery

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Penile fracture is a medical emergency, despite there being no bone in the penis. Sudden bending can tear the tissue that supports an erection and sometimes injure the urinary tube. Rapid assessment and treatment offer the best chance of avoiding lasting problems. This article explains what to recognize and what hospital care may involve; it should never delay urgent help.

Suspected penile fracture needs emergency care

A penile fracture is an urgent injury to the erect penis. If it bends suddenly and you develop pain, swelling, bruising or a rapid loss of erection, go to an emergency department immediately. Do not wait for a routine appointment, a photograph review or symptoms to settle.

Stop sexual activity. Do not bend, massage or try to straighten the injured penis, and do not test whether another erection is possible. Embarrassment should not delay care. Even if the injury happened earlier and you have not yet sought help, get assessed; a delay does not make treatment pointless.

What tears if there is no bone?

The penis has no bone. Its paired erectile chambers, the corpora cavernosa, fill with blood during erection. A strong fibrous covering called the tunica albuginea surrounds them; a penile fracture is a tear in this covering, often with injury to the underlying erectile tissue.

The urethra, the tube carrying urine out of the body, may be injured as well. That is why treatment considers both erections and urination. An ordinary bruise and a true fracture can look similar from the outside and need professional assessment to distinguish them.

Warning signs and possible urethral injury

A cracking or popping sound, immediate loss of erection, pain and rapidly developing swelling or dark bruising are typical warning signs. The penis may bend or look misshapen. Not everyone has every feature, so the absence of a sound does not safely rule out injury.

Tell the emergency team about blood at the urinary opening, blood in the urine, pain when urinating or difficulty passing urine. These can indicate a urethral injury. Inability to urinate is especially important; do not put anything into the urethra or attempt a catheter yourself.

Other injuries, such as a torn superficial vein or ligament, can also cause bruising. You cannot reliably decide at home which injury it is or whether an operation is needed. A reduction in pain does not establish that the deeper tissues are intact.

How the injury happens

The usual mechanism is a sudden forceful bend or impact while the penis is erect. It can happen during intercourse if the penis slips out and strikes the partner’s body, during vigorous masturbation, when rolling onto an erection, or after another accident or blow.

No sexual position makes injury impossible. Different studies report different circumstances; a simple ranking of positions cannot predict an individual injury. Focus on avoiding sudden bending and uncontrolled force rather than blaming either partner.

Examination, imaging and urine tests

The clinician asks when and how the injury happened and examines swelling, bruising and deformity. A clear history and examination can be enough to identify a fracture. Ultrasound may help in an uncertain case, with MRI used selectively when doubt remains and it is available. Imaging should not delay necessary surgery when the diagnosis is clear.

Cavernosography uses injected contrast to image the erectile chambers. It is a specialized option mentioned in trauma guidance, not a routine test that every patient needs. The treating team selects investigations according to the findings and local expertise.

A urine sample can show blood, but it is not the same as imaging the urethra. If urethral injury is suspected, a retrograde urethrogram uses contrast introduced through the urinary opening and X-rays; a flexible camera examination may also be used, including during surgery. Explain urinary symptoms so the team can choose the appropriate assessment.

Why prompt surgical repair is usually recommended

For a confirmed fracture, urological guidance recommends prompt surgery to close the torn tunica with stitches and repair associated injuries when necessary. The aim is to preserve comfortable erections and urinary function and reduce later curvature or scarring.

A superficial injury without a tunical tear may have a different treatment plan after assessment. This does not mean that rest, ice or painkillers are a safe substitute for emergency evaluation of a suspected fracture. The surgeon will explain the procedure, anaesthetic, possible catheter and individual risks.

Recovery and follow-up

Hospital stay and healing time depend on the injury, the repair and whether the urethra was involved. Some people go home relatively soon, while others need a longer stay or a catheter. Follow the team’s instructions for dressings, prescribed medicines, activity and catheter care; do not remove a catheter yourself.

Follow-up checks wound healing, urination and sexual function. Additional scans or urethral tests are selected when needed, rather than promised for everyone. Contact the service for increasing pain, fever, wound redness or discharge, significant bleeding or urinary problems; inability to pass urine needs urgent care.

When can sexual activity resume?

Wait for the surgical team’s clearance before intercourse or masturbation. Advice depends on healing and the extent of repair. BAUS patient information advises avoiding all sexual activity for six weeks; a generic one-month date is not permission to restart in your own case.

An erection occurring during recovery does not prove that the repair is ready for sexual activity. Ask what to do about painful erections and when to return to exercise, work and sex. Do not use medicines or devices to test the repair without the treating team’s advice.

Longer-term outlook and reducing future injury

Prompt treatment generally improves the outlook, but no success percentage guarantees an individual result. Curvature, painful erections, scar tissue, erection difficulties or urinary narrowing can occur after the injury or repair. Report persistent or new problems at follow-up; further care may help.

Use adequate compatible lubricant and controlled movements, and pause to guide the penis if it slips out or you change position. Avoid deliberate bending, forceful manipulation or pressing an erection into restrictive clothing. These precautions reduce avoidable force but cannot guarantee prevention.

An injury can affect confidence and relationships as well as the body. Ask for support if worry or distress persists. Be honest with clinicians about what happened; the purpose is appropriate treatment, not judgment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Suspected fracture requires immediate emergency assessment; do not postpone care for embarrassment or self-treatment.

Clinical examination is central; imaging and urethral investigations are selected according to uncertainty and associated injury.

Prompt repair is recommended for confirmed fracture, with attention to urinary as well as erectile function.

Recovery and return to sex require the treating team’s instructions; published timelines are not individual clearance.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you prepare questions about follow-up and recovery. It cannot rule out a fracture from a photograph, assess urethral injury or clear you to resume sex. Seek emergency care before using an app to document an acute injury.

When to seek help

A suspected penile fracture needs immediate emergency care. Stop sexual activity and do not straighten, massage or test the injured penis. Blood at the urinary opening or inability to urinate must be reported urgently. This information does not replace emergency assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Go to an emergency department immediately for a suspected penile fracture.
  • A missing popping sound or improving pain does not safely exclude serious injury.
  • Report blood at the urinary opening, blood in urine or trouble urinating.
  • Clinicians choose imaging and urethral tests; clear fractures usually need prompt repair.
  • Resume sex only with individualized surgical advice and attend follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

What should I do if I think I have a penile fracture?

Stop sexual activity and go to an emergency department immediately. Do not wait for bruising to worsen, try to straighten the penis or test another erection. Seek assessment even if you delayed initially.

Does a penile fracture mean a bone has broken?

No. The penis has no bone. The injury is a tear in the strong covering of the erectile chambers, and the underlying tissue or urethra may also be injured.

Do I need every symptom to seek help?

No. A pop, sudden loss of erection, pain, swelling or bruising after bending are warning signs, but not every person has all of them. Tell clinicians about urinary symptoms or bleeding.

Is a urine test the same as a retrograde urethrogram?

No. A urine sample checks for findings such as blood. A retrograde urethrogram is a contrast X-ray examination of the urethra. The team decides whether it or a camera examination is needed.

Can a true fracture heal with ice alone?

Do not rely on home treatment. Confirmed fractures usually need prompt surgical repair. Other bruising injuries may be managed differently only after assessment.

Can I have sex a month after surgery?

Do not use one month as automatic clearance. Follow the surgeon’s plan; BAUS patient guidance advises six weeks without intercourse or masturbation, and some injuries may need a different recovery period.

Does surgery guarantee normal erections?

No. Prompt repair improves the outlook, but curvature, pain, erection or urinary problems can still occur. Follow-up is important, and ongoing symptoms should be discussed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
